item.title: 'Woke' Smithsonian exhibit lionizes embattled Fauci amid conservative scrutiny of museum's messaging
item.description: Anthony Fauci's signed baseball cap and heroic placard are prominently displayed at the Smithsonian as the White House scrutinizes the museum's messaging.
item.content:encoded:
The embattled former face of the United States' COVID-19 response is prominently displayed and heroically framed at the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History — as the network of Smithsonian institutions face scrutiny over woke messaging from government officials.

Dr. Anthony Fauci, formerly the head of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID), has a prominent place at the museum's "Entertainment Nation" exhibit.

"As a deadly pandemic ravaged the nation, major sports leagues found themselves at the center of a debate over 'reopening' the country," a placard dedicated to Fauci says.

FAUCI'S NEWLY RELEASED COVID DIARIES REVEAL BIZARRE FIXATION ON FAME AS PANDEMIC DEATHS MOUNTED

"Amidst a cacophony of misinformation and denial, advice from Dr. Anthony Fauci, the nation’s leading epidemiologist, urged leagues to make decisions about resuming play 'based on scientific evidence and public health judgment,'" it continues. "When baseball became the first league to retake the field, Fauci threw the ceremonial opening pitch—wearing a facemask in a stadium empty of fans."

A diary kept by Fauci while the pandemic raged, recently exposed by Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., shows a man fixated on his own fame, who acknowledged answers to controversial questions in private, but said the opposite in public.

One of those controversial questions dealt with the origin of the virus. COVID-19 may have originated in a National Institute of Health (NIH) funded facility in China. While Fauci recognized privately that the virus may have accidentally escaped a lab, he stalwartly maintained the opposite in public. Fauci critics who suggested otherwise, including other doctors, were castigated. Fauci also insisted that the government was not conducting controversial gain-of-function research. That was later proved false.

FAUCI PRIVATELY TOOK CREDIT FOR COVID-19 LOCKDOWNS DESPITE PUBLIC DENIAL, NEWLY EXPOSED DIARY ENTRIES REVEAL

Alongside the Smithsonian's heroic characterization of Fauci as a man of science, the museum prominently features that Washington Nationals baseball cap, signed by the doctor, that he wore while throwing out the first pitch when MLB resumed play after lockdowns.

Fauci also repeatedly denied that he was behind the damaging pandemic-era lockdowns, but acknowledged in his diary that mayors and health officials in the country's largest metropolitan areas, including New York City and Los Angeles, were taking his advice to shut their municipalities down.

Diary posts also show that the doctor, often framed as a humble lifelong public servant, was obsessed with the attention he received during the pandemic. He extensively documented flattering news stories about himself, bragging in May of 2020 that his "national and international fame is explosive and really unimaginable" and that it was "not hyperbole" to say he was "the most famous and talked about person in the country."

TRUMP ORDERS SIGNS OUTSIDE SMITHSONIAN MUSEUM AMID ROW OVER ITS DEPICTION OF AMERICAN HISTORY

The pandemic claimed 1.2 million American lives.

Fauci was grilled on Capitol Hill Wednesday before the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, chaired by Paul. He invoked his Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination 111 times, failing to answer a single question.

The Smithsonian is dealing with government scrutiny of its own, both from congress and the White House.

The American History museum's director, Anthea Hartig, was grilled before Congress last week over sexually explicit imagery, Mickey Mouse being linked to racism and a museum toolkit discussing "objectivity" as a feature of White supremacy.

The museum's MASS Action Toolkit, a mid-2010s anthology for museums that references the 2014 Ferguson, Missouri, police shooting of Mike Brown and subsequent Black Lives Matter protests. It links politeness and being on time to white supremacy.

The White House chastised the taxpayer-funded museum for pushing "one-sided, divisive political narratives."

"American taxpayers should not be funding institutions that undermine our country or promote one-sided, divisive political narratives," White House official Lindsey Halligan told Fox News Digital. "The Smithsonian Institution should present history in a way that is accurate, balanced, and consistent with the values that make the United States of America exceptional."

The White House also released a report on July 4 that criticized the Smithsonian's portrayal of American history, and more recently, President Donald Trump ordered the National Park Service to place signs outside the museum directing visitors and passersby to an online resource that he says portrays an "accurate" version of American history.

He also blasted the museum as "woke" and "OUT OF CONTROL" on TRUTH Social.

Fox News' Charles Creitz and Jasmine Baehr contributed to this report.

item.title: New audio released following Nolan Wells disappearance doesn't show 'anything nefarious': retired FBI agent
item.description: A Sea Tow audio recording captures the frantic call from teens on a sinking boat at Horn Island the night Nolan Wells went missing on July 4.
item.content:encoded:
A retired FBI agent says that new audio released following Nolan Wells' disappearance and death doesn't show "anything nefarious."

Wells, 18, went missing July 4 after a boat trip with friends to Horn Island, a barrier island off Mississippi's Gulf Coast. Crews searched the area for two days before a National Parks Service ranger found his remains on the island's northwestern tip on July 6.

Wells' friends returned to the mainland that afternoon without him. Jackson County Sheriff John Ledbetter has said investigators believe Wells chose to remain on the island, and it wasn't until later that night that his mother learned from one of his friends he was missing, prompting her to report it to authorities.

Fox News Digital obtained a recording of a call made to Sea Tow on the evening of July 4 by someone aboard the boat, who said the vessel was taking on water as it prepared to return to the mainland. The individual said there were seven people onboard.

SEARCH CALLED OFF AFTER BODY MATCHING MISSING TEEN NOLAN WELLS FOUND OFF MISSISSIPPI COAST

"Hey, we’re at the west tip of Horn, and our bilge pump stopped working. We’re sinking. Can y’all please come?" an individual can be heard saying to the Sea Tow dispatcher.

When the dispatcher asked how far the water is coming inside the boat, the individual replied, "It’s coming up... we’re just sinking. I don’t know. We’re going down though."

"And is everyone on board and in good health otherwise?" the dispatcher asked.

"Yeah, everyone is on board," the individual on the boat responded.

The man heard talking to the Sea Tow dispatcher requested someone to come help un-sink the boat and get it towed back to the Fort Bayou launch in Ocean Springs, Mississippi.

NOLAN WELLS INDEPENDENT AUTOPSY DOESN'T POINT TO FOUL PLAY, FORMER MEDICAL EXAMINER SAYS

The Sea Tow dispatcher spoke with a separate boat captain, who said he was on the phone with the boat's owner.

"It sounds like a bunch of kids on board on Horn Island," the dispatcher said. "He’s saying the boat is sinking and he’s on Horn Island... It’s just unfortunate, he’s just a kid... there’s a lot going on... I’m guessing they’re all under 18... He wants you guys to go out there and un-pump the boat and then tow it in?"

The dispatcher then spoke with a captain, who said he was already on the phone with a man who owned the boat, a relative of the teen who called, and said those on the boat were in a "panic" because the boat wouldn't crank.

"It sounds like a bunch of kids on board on Horn Island," the dispatcher told the captain. "He’s saying the boat is sinking and he’s on Horn Island. It’s just unfortunate, he’s just a kid. It’s a lot going on.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

"He wants you guys to go out there and un-pump the boat and then tow it in," the dispatcher said.

The captain said the boat's owner told him the teens didn't "need any help right now, but if something changes, he'll call me back."

FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

Sea Tow didn't end up towing the boat.

Former FBI agent Jonathan Gilliam told Fox News Digital he doesn't believe the Sea Tow audio points to any signs of foul play, as some people on social media have claimed.

WATCH: Retired FBI agent says nothing 'nefarious' in newly released Nolan Wells boat audio

GOT A TIP?

"I don't hear anything nefarious... it just sounded like there was a lot of stuff going on, that they were taking on water — not panic as much as this young person was trying to resolve a situation in a party atmosphere."

Gilliam also pointed out that the call itself undercuts the idea of a cover-up.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

"By the way, they're taking on water. They're going to be calling for assistance, which could lead to authorities. If they had done something, that'd be a very bad time for a person who'd done something nefarious to call out people and for them to get away with something. So I don't think it added anything to the conspiracies of something having occurred knowingly in a nefarious manner."

Several of Wells' friends told authorities he "chose to remain at the island" with an unidentified female rather than return to the mainland with the group he arrived with, according to a Mississippi Department of Marine Resources police report obtained by Fox News Digital.

GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL

According to the police report, authorities "did not have reason to believe there were any water related exigencies or emergencies and he believed the most likely scenario was Nolan rode in on another vessel but did not have his phone in his possession to make contact with family."

During a July 22 news conference, attorney Ben Crump revealed that an area of "red discoloration" was found on Wells' head, but said Dr. Roger Mitchell, who performed an independent autopsy, couldn't come to a conclusion on a cause or manner of death "pending further investigation." An official autopsy into Wells' death hasn't been completed.

Wells was a wide receiver at Southwest Mississippi Community College and had hopes to play at the Division 1 level, according to Crump, an attorney for his family.

item.title: Trump accused China of an 'election security nightmare' but then undercut his own warning
item.description: Trump said China's voter file collection happened "a long time ago" and suggested both nations spy on each other as Xi Jinping's September visit proceeds.
item.content:encoded:
Less than two weeks after accusing China of carrying out an "unprecedented election security nightmare," President Donald Trump has not changed his posture toward Beijing and is moving ahead with plans to host Chinese President Xi Jinping in September.

"This data loss presents an unprecedented election security nightmare," Trump said in a July 16 address. "The intelligence even shows that China assigned a data exploitation unit specifically to this new project."

Intelligence officials, he said, "worked to actively suppress and downplay information about the extent of China’s sinister election meddling."

TRUMP’S UPBEAT CHINA MESSAGE COLLIDES WITH DEEPENING BEIJING RIVALRY

Trump did not claim China changed votes or altered election results. Instead, he argued Beijing engaged in an influence campaign aimed at shaping U.S. public perceptions.

But within days of the address, Trump undercut the urgency of his own warning. Asked whether China would face consequences, he said the alleged activity "took place a long time ago" and suggested it reflected the broader intelligence rivalry between the two countries.

"They do things and we do things to them," Trump said July 21 in remarks to reporters. "I’ll be honest, we do things to them, too. It’s not a one-way street."

So far, the fallout has been directed almost entirely inward. Trump ordered investigations into U.S. officials who handled the intelligence, while his trade and diplomatic engagement with Beijing has continued largely unchanged.

Trump’s posture toward TikTok has undergone a similar shift. He sought to ban the platform during his first term over national-security concerns tied to its Chinese ownership but joined it during the 2024 campaign. Five days after Trump’s address, most Cabinet members launched official accounts after the Justice Department cleared federal employees to use TikTok under its new U.S.-controlled ownership.

It also remains unclear when Trump first learned of the intelligence or whether he knew about it before traveling to Beijing in May. A White House official confirmed Xi's Sept. 24 visit will proceed but did not answer questions about when Trump was briefed or whether anyone accused of withholding the intelligence remains in government.

The Chinese embassy could not immediately be reached for comment on the planned visit.

Newly declassified records released by the administration provide fresh details about China’s alleged collection and analysis of American voter information and reveal an internal intelligence debate over whether Beijing’s broader activities amounted to election interference. But the documents also establish less than some of Trump’s rhetoric appeared to suggest.

CHINA DISMISSES TRUMP ELECTION INTERFERENCE ACCUSATIONS AS 'ENTIRELY FABRICATED,' THREATENS COUNTERMEASURES

During the July 16 address, Trump said China had acquired 220 million U.S. voter files containing names, addresses, phone numbers and political affiliations. He said Beijing assigned a unit to exploit the information and which had the potential to use it to register voters or engage in other "nefarious activities."

Trump called the findings "stunning" and the broader vulnerabilities "a cyber threat aimed at the very heart of our democracy."

The president accused intelligence officials of working to "actively suppress and downplay" China’s "sinister election meddling." He cited an internal message saying officials had "deliberately massaged" a pending President’s Daily Brief and another in which an FBI official described "running a shadow government."

'SHADOW GOVERNMENT': TRUMP CLAIMS INTEL COMMUNITY BRAGGED ABOUT HIDING CHINESE MEDDLING

Trump directed the Justice Department, FBI, CIA and Office of the Director of National Intelligence to investigate. He said those responsible should be fired and potentially prosecuted.

The roughly 270 pages of released records show that Chinese entities amassed and analyzed large quantities of American voter information.

The figure at the center of Trump’s announcement appears to come from a record showing that a Chinese entity possessed an unspecified dataset containing approximately 204.8 million American voter records. The document does not identify its source or explain how it was obtained.

Other records describe China analyzing registration information from 18 states and a Chinese actor downloading publicly available historical voter information from six states. The documents do not show that China altered voter rolls, changed ballots or penetrated vote-counting systems.

The documents also include a raw FBI report alleging that China planned to manufacture fraudulent U.S. driver’s licenses that could be used to cast mail ballots for Joe Biden. The allegation came from a single uncorroborated source, and the report was recalled the day it was distributed and never reissued.

There was no evidence that any fraudulent votes were actually cast.

Emily Harding, director of the Intelligence, National Security, and Technology Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, wrote that China "likely gained little advantage" from voter records that were largely publicly available or available for purchase.

Harding wrote that the internal exchanges showed "an honest, and valuable, analytical debate" rather than a cover-up. She noted that the recalled FBI report relied on unreliable third-hand information and said references to the election were removed from one briefing so a specialized election-security team could address the issue.

Trump did not explain which American activities he considered comparable to China’s collection and analysis of voter information.

There is some public record behind Trump’s suggestion that the intelligence competition runs both ways — but China does not hold free national elections.

Trump authorized the CIA in 2019 to conduct a covert influence campaign against China, Reuters reported in 2024. According to three former U.S. officials, operatives used false online identities to circulate damaging but fact-based information about Xi’s government and attempt to shape public opinion inside China.

The CIA declined to confirm the program. Documents leaked by former National Security Agency contractor Edward Snowden also showed the National Security Agency penetrating Chinese networks, including the systems of telecommunications giant Huawei.

Trump expressed a similar view during his May visit to Beijing, although he was speaking then about Chinese espionage more broadly.

"They spy on us," Trump told Fox News host Sean Hannity during the trip. "We spy on them too, I guess."

Trump otherwise used the visit to promote closer economic ties. He traveled with leading American executives, called Xi a "great leader" and said it was an "honor" to be his friend.

The White House later announced that the two countries had agreed to establish boards of trade and investment. China also committed to purchase 200 Boeing aircraft and at least $17 billion in American agricultural products annually through 2028, according to the administration.

Preparations for Xi’s visit continued after Trump’s address.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio met Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi July 22 to lay the groundwork for what he called a "very positive" visit but said Trump’s election allegations were not discussed. Rubio added that it would be "reckless and irresponsible" for the two powers not to maintain a relationship.

China has denied interfering in the 2020 election. Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lin Jian called the allegations "entirely fabricated" and urged the United States to stop using China as an election issue.

item.title: Trump tells foreign students: overstay your visa, face the consequences
item.description: Foreign students dragging out degrees while working illegally or filing frivolous asylum claims face new accountability under a final administrative rule.
item.content:encoded:
Amid all the noise in Washington and simultaneous lack of legislation coming out of Congress, there have been some quiet wins for accountability in our visa system.

One recent win is an administrative final rule that requires foreign students to comply with their visas. Administrative rules govern how the government implements the law in practice.

Most foreign students who qualify get an F-1 visa, which allows them to study at the undergraduate or graduate level. Some get a J-1, which is for international exchange visitors.

RUBIO PUSHES BACK ON INDIA'S CONCERNS OVER US VISA CURBS, SAYS POLICY MUST BE 'AMERICA FIRST' UNDER TRUMP

When student visa holders arrive here, they are given permission to enter under what’s called "duration of status." That means that as long as they are full-time students, they can stay.

An earlier rule allows students, while still on their student visas, to work in "Optional Practical Training" for a year, with another two years if they have STEM degrees. The definition of STEM is 16 pages long and generous. Because foreigners on OPT are working using their student visa (remember – "duration of status") their employers are not required to pay into Social Security and Medicare. That’s a discount of up to 15% for hiring foreign workers instead of Americans.

"Duration of status" combined with OPT incentivizes marginal students not to complete their degrees in due course and, as they originally claimed they would, go home.

TRUMP ADMINISTRATION ORDERS GREEN CARD APPLICANTS TO LEAVE THE US, APPLY FROM THEIR HOME COUNTRIES

The education-migration complex is desperate to keep the foreign student gravy train on the rails. They make the new rule seem as if it is cutting off opportunity. Quite the opposite: it’s about asking for responsibility.

It’s not hard to complete a bachelor’s degree in four years, especially for foreign students. Americans can apply to college knowing they’ll need to work or apply for aid and grants. Foreigners, meanwhile, are required to show consular officers in their visa interview that they can afford the entire course of study, including tuition, lodging and incidental costs. They are not, in theory, supposed to work.

If they decide to earn a master’s after their BA, or even a PhD, the new rule just means they have to go home, apply for a new visa, and show the consular officer they are credible students, can afford the entire course of study and intend to return home when done.

TRUMP PUTS ASYLUM LAWYERS ‘ON NOTICE’ WITH NEW FRONT IN WAR ON FRAUD

That’s what is really freaking out the edu-crats. Many foreign students intend to stay in the U.S. Some never go to school at all; these get dropped from the Student and Exchange Visitor Information System (SEVIS) maintained by DHS. They should then be deported, but many make frivolous asylum claims to remain.

Others do go to school, but drag it out over many years, taking minimal classes to maintain status while working, often illegally. Schools don’t mind, as long as the fees keep coming.

But we should mind. America doesn’t need to import this type of low-motivation student.

What America needs even less are students who come here pre-programmed with hostility to the United States, Western civilization and capitalism, who spend their time protesting on campus.

Some foreign students on campuses across the United States have been here for years, spending far too much time and energy protesting Israel, capitalism, ICE and Western civilization instead of hitting the books and getting a degree. These permanent students aren’t adding to our national prosperity, security, or unity.

America wants students who come, study and finish their degrees. The left will tell you that foreign students are all the best of the best. Not so. As a consular officer, I did thousands of student visa applications in Africa, Asia and Europe. I’ve seen everything from applicants with full scholarships at MIT and Harvard to those wanting to study English at a community college near their uncle, who just happens to own a motel or gas station.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

America welcomes legitimate students. We will always have room for the most talented and entrepreneurial to stay. But our universities are not there to facilitate mass economic migration.

The unemployment rate for recent American college graduates is 5.7%, higher than the national average. They need our support, not millions of foreign graduates to compete with.

The new rule on student visas is timely and welcome. Future presidents would be wise to keep it instead of caving to the education and migration lobby.

item.title: Daily eating habit linked to better brain health in older adults, new research suggests
item.description: A six-month trial found that older women who ate within eight to nine hours daily showed cognitive improvements beyond what weight loss alone provided.
item.content:encoded:
Eating within a shorter daily window could help support brain health as people age, according to new research.

Preliminary findings presented at NUTRITION 2026 — the American Society for Nutrition’s annual meeting in Maryland — suggests that older women who ate within eight to nine hours per day saw slight cognitive improvement compared to those who spread their meals over about 12 hours each day.

The small six-month trial included 47 postmenopausal obese or overweight women aged 50 to 79. They were each advised to reduce their daily food intake by about 500 calories.

INTERMITTENT FASTING'S REAL BENEFIT MAY COME AFTER YOU START EATING AGAIN

The participants were divided into two groups. One ate in a time-restricted window within an average of 8.2 hours, usually from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. The other group ate across a 12.3-hour window, according to a news release.

Both groups lost about 15 pounds over six months, but those in the shorter eating-window group performed better on cognitive tests measuring spatial planning and problem-solving.

The shorter-window group also showed fewer errors on memory and learning tests, but no meaningful differences in reaction time or multi-tasking ability.

PEOPLE LOST WEIGHT WHILE EATING SIGNIFICANTLY MORE FOOD — HERE'S THE SECRET

"These outcomes suggest a better ability to remember information during everyday tasks and reduce mistakes related to memory, attention and problem-solving," lead researcher Sue Shapses, PhD, a professor at Rutgers University and Rutgers-RWJ Medical Center, said in a press release. "Reductions in the eating window predicted greater improvements."

Although the pilot study included only a small number of participants, the researchers believe that time-restricted eating may support brain health by regulating circadian rhythm, reducing inflammation and improving metabolic health.

Losing weight alone can help "ward off some of the aging-related cognitive decline," according to Shapses.

"And these data suggest there may be additional benefits if you stop eating four hours prior to going to sleep and reduce food intake to eight to nine hours per day, compared to the usual eating window of 12 hours per day."

Women, as well as adults who are overweight or obese, tend to face a higher likelihood of developing Alzheimer’s disease and other forms of dementia as they age, according to the researchers.

Lauri Wright, PhD, director of nutrition programs and associate professor at the USF College of Public Health, who was not involved in this research, reflected on these findings in an interview with Fox News Digital.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"This is an interesting study because it suggests that when we eat may matter in addition to what and how much we eat," she said. "That suggests meal timing itself may have played a role, not just weight loss."

"The results are promising, but we need larger, longer studies before recommending time-restricted eating specifically to improve brain health."

Experts are still learning about how intermittent fasting affects the brain, although "several biological mechanisms are being considered," Wright noted.

"Giving the body a longer overnight break from eating may improve insulin sensitivity, reduce chronic inflammation, support healthy circadian rhythms and allow cells more time for repair and maintenance," she said. "Those processes are all linked to healthy brain aging."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

From a practical standpoint, eating within a shorter daily window often leads people to consume fewer calories, which can promote weight loss, according to New York-based certified holistic nutritionist Robin DeCicco.

IMAGE

"We know that maintaining a healthy weight helps with virtually everything," she told Fox News Digital. "Eating within a restricted window helps people cut calories."

"When you fast or ... have periods of time where you're not just eating throughout the whole day, it does help to lower markers of inflammation and certain sources of oxidative stress."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Many people have reported "feeling better" when fasting, DeCicco noted — especially those who have inflammatory conditions, which can include neurological disorders like Alzheimer’s and dementia.

"When you're fasting, you're giving your organs a chance to rest, you're giving the digestive system a chance to ‘rest and digest,’" she added.

Intermittent fasting isn’t the only way to support cognitive health, Wright countered.

"Regular physical activity, adequate sleep, controlling blood pressure and blood sugar, avoiding smoking, maintaining social connections and following an overall healthy dietary pattern, such as the Mediterranean diet, have much stronger evidence for protecting cognitive function over time," she said. "Think of meal timing as one potential piece of the puzzle rather than a magic bullet."

Intermittent fasting "isn’t appropriate for everyone," Wright warned, adding that she would advise against it for children and teens, pregnant or breastfeeding women, anyone with a history of an eating disorder, and people with diabetes who are taking insulin.

DeCicco agreed that fasting should be recommended and monitored by a medical professional, especially for those who take certain medications or have certain conditions.

item.title: Huckabee warns of 'biblical ignorance' as he defends conservative support for Israel
item.description: Mike Huckabee says "America First has never meant America only" and warns that biblical ignorance is fueling right-wing skepticism of Israel.
item.content:encoded:
As some on the right become more skeptical of the U.S.-Israel relationship, U.S. Ambassador Mike Huckabee warns that the trepidation is fueled by what he calls "biblical ignorance" and a misunderstanding of what it means to be "America First."

Speaking to Fox News Digital ahead of the 15th anniversary of the U.S. Israel Education Association's founding, Huckabee rejected the idea that putting America first means pushing away allies. Rather, he argued that support for Israel is aligned with U.S. interests and the religious convictions held by many Christians.

"When I look at the things on the right what I see is that there's biblical ignorance," Huckabee said. "People who say, 'you know, God has no longer got a promise that he's keeping to the Jewish people,' and I'm thinking 'well, that's news to God because he doesn't break a promise."

CHRISTIAN LEADERS HOLD EMERGENCY SUMMIT IN JERUSALEM TO CONFRONT GLOBAL RISE IN ANTISEMITISM

"If God broke his promise to the Jews, then what makes me, as a Christian, think that he won't break his promise to me?" he added.

In addition to being the former governor of Arkansas, Huckabee was also ordained as a Baptist minister and served as President of the Arkansas Baptist State Convention, giving him a perspective shaped by both politics and faith.

The ambassador also dismissed notions that Christians are not welcomed or allowed to worship freely in Israel. He told Fox News Digital that he plays bass guitar in his church praise band every Sunday and that "nobody throws a chair at me."

Skepticism and outright hostility toward Israel has become more prevalent in recent years in some corners of right-wing media and among more heterodox podcast stars, such as Joe Rogan, who said Wednesday that there was no doubt Israel was guilty of "genocide" in Gaza.

TRUMP THREATENS 'MAJOR MILITARY PUNISHMENT' FOR IRAN OVER FUTURE HOUTHI ATTACKS

However, the ambassador's concerns go beyond theological debates. Huckabee argued that some conservatives have misinterpreted the "America First" movement as one of pure isolationism.

"There's another thing on the right that I'm concerned about. People who say, 'Look, I'm an America First person,' I say 'I am too.' I was MAGA before anybody knew what MAGA was," Huckabee told Fox News Digital. "America First has never meant America only."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

The ambassador explained that America's interests do not stop at its borders, particularly when it comes to combatting enemy threats.

He pointed to Iran, saying that the regime has spent decades calling for "death to America." Huckabee also cited Iranian proxies across the globe and the threats they pose as key reasons why the U.S. cannot afford to ignore what happens overseas. For Huckabee, the threats emanating from Iran and its proxies reinforce his belief that putting America first does not mean turning inward.

"They've never changed their message that they want to murder us. So, when people tell you for 47 years their goal is to kill you, you're pretty stupid if you don't pay attention to that, and even more stupid if you do nothing about it," he said.

item.title: Don't let fake election websites fool you before 2026 midterms
item.description: Over 62,000 election-named domains were tracked since September 2025, with some active storefronts copying campaign branding to collect donations.
item.content:encoded:
You spot a campaign shirt online that makes you laugh. The site carries the candidate's name. It also has polished product photos and a familiar checkout page. So, you assume the store supports the campaign.

A fake election website can copy enough campaign cues to make that assumption feel reasonable. Your money and personal information could then reach an operator with no verified campaign connection.

New research provided to CyberGuy by WhoisXML API, an internet intelligence company that analyzes domain, IP and DNS data, tracked 62,081 election-named domains created since September 2025. Researchers identified 13,645 addresses that read like campaign sites based on their names.

The research classifies only a portion of the domains as campaign-style addresses. Legitimate campaigns, supporters, merchants and domain investors may control many of them. However, researchers also found live storefronts that used candidates' names while selling merchandise and accepting donation-style payments. That smaller group creates the clearest risk for you.

FAKE PASSWORD-MANAGER ALERTS COULD PUT YOUR VAULT AT RISK

CyberGuy Live: Missed "Sick of Spam?" Get the replay and checklist

Our free CyberGuy Live class, "Sick of Spam?", has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our spam-stopping checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you step by step through simple ways to reduce robocalls, spam texts, junk email and unwanted messages. You’ll also learn how to curb political texts, clean up your inbox and spot messages that could put your personal information at risk.

Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.

Why fake election websites surge before the midterms

National elections create a rush for online real estate. Campaign teams want memorable web addresses before someone else claims them. Supporters may launch fan pages, while merchants see an opportunity to sell political products. Impersonators can follow the same naming formula.

According to WhoisXML API, nearly 46% of the curated campaign-style set used structures such as "[name]for[office]" or "for[state]." Domains referencing congressional races appeared most often. Senate-themed names came next. State names also appeared across about one-third of the curated set. Texas led with 537 registrations. Florida, Georgia, Ohio and Colorado followed.

Those names feel familiar because real campaigns use the same structure. As a result, a questionable domain can look credible before you open the page. Across the domains studied, researchers said 90% hid the registrant's identity. In addition, 88% carried a one-year registration term. Privacy protection and short registration terms can have legitimate uses. Still, those details deserve more attention when a new site also copies campaign branding or asks for money.

A small change in a domain can hide in plain sight. WhoisXML API highlighted massiemoneybomb[.]us, which closely resembled the established massiemoneybomb[.]com fundraising address. The main difference appeared after the final dot.

That change may look obvious on a large computer screen. However, it becomes easier to miss on a phone, especially when a text or social media post opens the page directly. Researchers also examined kenpaxton[.]us. They said the domain was 58 days old when captured, while kenpaxton[.]com dated back to 2008.

The newer site reportedly sold supportive campaign products alongside merchandise criticizing the same candidate. That unusual mix offers a clue that the store may lack an official connection. Yet many shoppers will focus on the product photos or the price. A polished checkout can make the entire operation feel established. Alexandre François, the WhoisXML API domain scam researcher behind the study, told CyberGuy that AI can help operators build convincing websites quickly and at scale. That makes it even harder to judge a campaign page by its appearance alone.

Political merchandise may cost you more than the price on the screen. According to the research, some storefronts allowed visitors to add donation-style payments of up to $1,000 to a shopping cart. The sites then processed the payment through their own checkout flows.

One store reportedly continued accepting a donation-style payment after the candidate's official ActBlue page stopped taking contributions. The checkout requested a full name, street address, email address and phone number. It also collected payment card details.

A familiar payment processor can make that form feel safe. However, its presence only shows how the payment moves through the checkout. It cannot confirm that the candidate authorized the store or that the campaign receives the money.

François said the study found no direct evidence that donors lost money or had their data misused. "Only the payment platforms could see whether a donor lost money or had data misused, and their data was not part of this study," he told CyberGuy. The findings support caution rather than a claim that every highlighted site committed fraud.

Domain registration records can expose useful clues before or after a website launches. Researchers can review the creation date, registrar, paid registration period and privacy status. Sometimes, the records also identify the owner or registrant country. However, each clue has limits.

Many legitimate website owners use privacy services to keep home addresses and contact details out of public databases. Campaigns may also register several defensive domains so impersonators cannot claim them first. A one-year registration term also appears across ordinary websites. Price and convenience often drive that choice.

The risk grows when several details point in the same direction. A nearly copied domain may lead to a new storefront with an unofficial donation flow. A mismatched disclaimer adds another concern.

For federal political committees, public websites generally need a disclaimer that identifies who paid for the communication. The wording may also state whether a candidate authorized it. The FEC explains that disclaimer requirements cover political committee websites and online fundraising communications. A disclaimer cannot guarantee honesty. Still, a missing or mismatched statement gives you a strong reason to leave the page and verify the site elsewhere.

Campaigns also face limits when trying to secure every possible variation of a candidate's name. François said they should consistently promote one official domain and one donation link. He added that "the realistic option is monitoring" because registering every possible look-alike domain would be impractical. Monitoring new registrations can help campaigns find look-alike sites during their first days online. Campaigns can then report suspicious pages to the registrar, hosting company or payment provider.

SAME-NAME CANDIDATE DISQUALIFIED FROM KEY SENATE RACE OVER ALLEGED DEM SCHEME TO CONFUSE VOTERS

Before you buy campaign merchandise or make a political contribution online, use these checks to confirm that the site connects to the candidate or committee you intend to support.

Avoid starting with a link from an unexpected text, email, online ad or social media comment. Instead, search for the candidate independently. Then compare the result with links from the candidate's verified social media account or established public profile. "No single sign is enough, so it's best to check a few together and to reach the page from the campaign's own channel," François told CyberGuy.

You can also use a personal data removal service to reduce the personal information available through data brokers and people-search sites. This may limit the details scammers can use to make unexpected messages, targeted ads or social media comments feel more convincing. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com.

For federal races, use the FEC's campaign finance database at fec.gov/data/ to look up candidates and registered committees. The database shows federal candidate and committee filings. For state or local races, check the appropriate state or local election authority. Many campaigns process contributions through ActBlue or WinRed. In those cases, the payment address should show secure.actblue.com or secure.winred.com. Some campaigns use other processors, so an unfamiliar payment provider alone does not prove the page is deceptive.

Tap or click the address bar before entering payment information. Check the spelling and domain ending. Then look for added words or letters that imitate the campaign's real address.

A scammer may replace ".com" with ".us." Another operator may add words such as "official," "store," "donate," or "support" to make the address feel authentic. François said the difference may also involve one word, a hyphen or an ending such as ".vote" or ".store."

Scroll to the bottom of the site and review the area around the donation form. A federal political committee website should identify who paid for the communication. Depending on the committee, the disclaimer may also explain whether the candidate authorized it.

Compare that committee name with the FEC database. Leave the page when the names conflict or the disclosure looks vague. Keep in mind that a deceptive page can copy a real committee's name. Treat the disclosure as one clue rather than proof that the page belongs to the campaign.

Open the candidate's established website in a separate tab. Look for a direct link to the merchandise store or donation page. If the official site sends you somewhere else, use the link it provides.

Also review the store's contact details and return policy. Be cautious if it sells products supporting a candidate alongside merchandise attacking that candidate. That unusual mix may signal the store has no official campaign connection. A page that keeps collecting contributions after a candidate withdraws also deserves closer scrutiny. The same applies when a store continues selling campaign merchandise after the official donation page closes.

The padlock in your browser means the site uses an encrypted connection. It offers no proof about the person or business behind the page.

CISA warns that phishing attacks may use malicious websites that impersonate trusted organizations to collect personal information. A professional design and secure connection still require you to verify the operator.

Pressure can push you past obvious warning signs. Be cautious when a site claims a donation match will disappear within minutes. A countdown clock that keeps resetting should also raise concern.

The FTC's broader donation-safety guidance recommends researching an organization and resisting pressure to give immediately.

WHAT A SCAMMER SEES THE MOMENT THEY GOOGLE YOUR NAME

A credit card generally offers stronger dispute protections than a debit card. It also keeps the payment away from funds in your checking account. The FTC says legal protections for credit cards exceed those for debit cards in billing disputes.

Save your receipt and take screenshots of the product page and checkout. Make sure the full domain appears in at least one image. After you pay, check your statement to confirm the amount and make sure the site did not enroll you in recurring contributions.

A fake campaign website may try to push a malicious download or send you to another harmful page. Strong antivirus software can help detect suspicious files and block some dangerous websites. However, you still need to verify the campaign connection before you pay. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.

If a store asks you to create an account, use a unique password. A password manager can generate and save a strong password for you, so you do not have to remember it. Reusing a password could put your other accounts at risk if the login information gets exposed. Turn on two-factor authentication (2FA) when the site offers it.

Election season gives questionable websites a powerful disguise. A candidate's name can create trust before you verify who operates the page. The scale of this research should make every online donor slow down. Researchers found more than 62,000 election-named domains, though many may serve legitimate purposes. The clearest concern comes from active storefronts that copy campaign-style branding and collect money outside a verified campaign path. Take an extra minute before buying a shirt or making a contribution. Find the official campaign site through a trusted source. Then confirm the web address and committee disclosure before you enter personal or payment information.

item.title: Nancy Guthrie case: Unclaimed $1.2M reward suggests 'very small circle' of suspects, retired FBI agent says
item.description: A retired FBI negotiator says the unclaimed $1.2 million reward in Nancy Guthrie's suspected abduction is a clue in and of itself six months after her kidnapping.
item.content:encoded:
EXCLUSIVE: TUCSON, Ariz. — The fact that a seven-figure reward remains unclaimed nearly six months after the suspected abduction of Nancy Guthrie from her home in Tucson's Catalina Foothills neighborhood tells one veteran investigator that if the masked intruder on her porch had help, it came from a small, tight-knit group.

"That tells me the circle who knows is very small, and whoever is in it is bound by something stronger than money: blood, fear, shared exposure," said Jason Pack, a retired FBI negotiator and supervisory agent who has been closely following the case. "Those bonds hold. Until they don't."

The more people who know about a crime, the more likely someone would come forward and claim the reward money, he said. The combined sum of rewards in the case is over $1.2 million — and none of it has been claimed 179 days after Guthrie's suspected abduction.

NANY GUTHRIE SHERIFF CHRIS NANOS SAYS HE'S 'STILL POSITIVE' CASE WILL BE RESOLVED DESPITE LONG WAIT

"Money like that usually pulls somebody loose from almost any group," Pack told Fox News Digital. "It hasn't."

Rather than a dead end, Pack sees the untouched reward as another clue.

"In my experience, a meaningful share of cases like this break sideways," he said. "Somebody gets arrested for something unrelated and starts talking. A relationship ends badly. Somebody's conscience finally outruns their fear. Six months is a long time to hold something this heavy, and the people around whoever did this have had six months to notice the change in them."

NANCY GUTHRIE CASE POINTS TO CRIMINAL UNDERWORLD 'WRENCH ATTACK' THEORY, RETIRED DETECTIVE SAYS

Pack said it looks like the abductor or abductors tried to plan the crime — and did it poorly. At least one suspect is believed to have cased out the house. He wore a ski mask, long sleeves and gloves, and covered the lens of her Nest doorbell camera — which was missing when police arrived the next day.

"When it went wrong, and I believe it went wrong fast, they had no plan for that either," he said. "Everything since reads to me like improvising around a failure, not professionals executing a plan."

Guthrie, the 84-year-old mother of "Today" co-host Savannah Guthrie, is dependent on heart medication and has a pacemaker. She has limited mobility — and a close-knit family.

SAVANNAH GUTHRIE'S EMOTIONAL PLEA TO MOM'S KIDNAPPER MAY SIGNAL 'NEW LINE OF COMMUNICATION': REPORT

"She had dinner with her family on a Saturday night, went home, and never made it to church the next morning," Pack said. "That's who we're talking about. Not a case number. A mother who was supposed to be at church."

FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

While the suspects made critical mistakes, he said, that doesn't mean the investigation has stalled.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

Pack also shared a direct message for Guthrie's neighbors and residents of the surrounding communities:

SEND US A TIP

"Go back and check your own cameras from that time period. Doorbell, security, dashcam," he said. "A lot of systems archive further back than people realize. If you drove through the area that night, pull your dashcam files."

If you saw something but don't have video, it's still worth speaking out, he said.

"And think about the people in your own life. Somebody who left town. Somebody whose behavior turned in February and never turned back," he said. "You don't have to be sure. That's not your job. Sorting it out is [the investigators' job]."

In May, a source with knowledge of the case told Fox News Digital that the FBI was bringing new technology into the investigation.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

Pima County Sheriff Chris Nanos, whose department is the lead agency, said in an interview this week that he still believes the case will be resolved.

"We have so much DNA to sort through," he said in an interview aired on "Today." "We have so much, in terms of video evidence, to look at."

And they've spent months learning things from the DNA and the video and other forensics that the public hasn't seen, Pack noted.

"I've watched cases break in month eight, month 14, month 30," said Pack, whose FBI career lasted 21 years, 11 of them as a negotiator. "Most every one of those families had stopped believing it was ever coming."

Anyone with information on the case is asked to dial 1-800-CALL-FBI. An anonymous reward can also be obtained by calling 520-88-CRIME with information that leads to an arrest in the case.

item.title: Shark Week fans may want to think twice before eating this ocean predator, experts warn
item.description: Shark meat offers high-quality protein but carries the highest mercury burden in the commercial market, plus arsenic and neurotoxin BMAA risks.
item.content:encoded:
It's Shark Week, and for all their mystery, power and danger, some shark species are also prized as seafood.

Shark is eaten in many parts of the world and is especially popular in Brazil, Iceland, South Korea, Japan, Spain and Portugal. While it's far less common in the United States due to sustainability and health concerns, it can still be found at some restaurants and seafood markets.

In many countries, shark meat is an inexpensive protein, with almost 18 grams of protein in an average 3-ounce raw portion, but it can also contain dangerous levels of toxins.

TENNIS GREAT RAFAEL NADAL SWEARS BY BREAKFAST WITH NUTRIENT-PACKED TINY FISH

"Shark meat does provide high-quality protein, along with nutrients such as selenium and certain B vitamins, making it a good source of lean protein. However, its drawbacks generally outweigh its benefits," Lisa Young, registered dietitian and adjunct professor of nutrition at New York University, told Fox News Digital.

"Because sharks are large, long-lived predators at the top of the food chain, they tend to accumulate high levels of mercury and other environmental contaminants over time," she said.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The lean, high-quality protein and valuable micronutrients, including selenium, B12, eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) that shark meat contains, also come with the highest mercury burden in the commercial market, Kantha Shelke, senior lecturer of food safety regulations at Johns Hopkins University in Maryland, told Fox News Digital.

"Nutritionally, one can get just as much or more from salmon and sardines but without the risk," Shelke said.

The high mercury concentration can adversely affect the central nervous system, especially the developing fetal brain, as well as pregnant and breastfeeding women and children.

"Sharks also contain arsenic, another dangerous [heavy-metal contaminant] to avoid," Shelke said.

"For healthy adults, shark should not be a regular part of the diet," Young said.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

"If someone chooses to eat it, it should be an occasional food rather than a staple. It's generally wiser to select lower-mercury seafood more often to meet the recommendation of eating seafood about twice a week."

Brazil has long been the world's top consumer of shark meat, National Geographic reported. A traditional delicacy in Iceland is hákarl, made by fermenting Greenland shark using a centuries-old preservation method that makes it safe to eat. 

It smells similar to cleaning products, thanks to its high ammonia content, according to National Geographic.

Overfishing has greatly depleted some shark populations overseas, but in the U.S., "shark fisheries are some of the most sustainable in the world," the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) reports.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Some shark species are sold as substitutes for other seafood and have been used in the U.S. in dishes such as fish and chips and fish pie, as well as in some imitation crab products, according to Tasting Table. It is also served during certain seasons on the Gulf Coast as grilled shark steaks or fried as shark bites or in tacos.

K&S Roti Shop and Jamaican Restaurant in Stratford, Connecticut, serves a traditional Caribbean dish from the island nation of Trinidad and Tobago that incorporates breaded shark meat. It's likely the only restaurant in the state to serve shark, Connecticut Insider reported.

Eating shark "as a one-time culinary experience for the novelty" is fine, Shelke said, but she cautioned not to exceed "your weekly mercury budget" by also eating tuna steak or swordfish that week.

"If pregnant, planning to be, breastfeeding or feeding children, please skip it," she said.

item.title: Smithsonian exec who said DEI 'must be at the center' of institutions is raking in eye-popping salary
item.description: Lonnie Bunch earned over $4.4 million from 2020-2024 while pushing DEAI and diversity initiatives at the taxpayer-funded Smithsonian Institution.
item.content:encoded:
FIRST ON FOX: Lonnie Bunch III, the Smithsonian Institution secretary who called DEI an "integral to excellence in museum practice," raked in over $4.4 million from 2020-2024 in base salary and added benefits, a Fox News Digital review found.

While the Smithsonian funds executive compensation through private trust revenues to comply with federal pay caps, the high-dollar package could draw fresh scrutiny because federal taxpayers still fund roughly 60% of the institution's overall budget.

During his tenure, Bunch has championed a sweeping transformation of the institution's cultural footprint, stating during a 2019 interview with the Smithsonian Magazine that he wanted the Smithsonian to make "diversity and inclusion so central that it’s no longer talked about."

"We call ourselves the Great Convener, but we’re really a great legitimizer. And I want the Smithsonian to legitimize important issues, whether it’s 1619 or climate change," Bunch said, referring to the controversial 1619 Project that has been repeatedly slammed for "egregious errors" by scholars. "We help people think about what’s important, what they should debate, what they should embrace."

FORMER DEMOCRATIC STAFFERS, DEI LEADERS SHAPE SMITHSONIAN LEADERSHIP AMID POLITICAL FIRESTORM

"Everybody that thought about the 1619 Project, whether they liked it or disagreed with it, saw that the Smithsonian had fingerprints on it. And that to me was a great victory," he added.

As secretary, Bunch reports to the organization’s board of regents and oversees the Smithsonian’s 21 museums, 21 libraries, the National Zoo and several research centers. Within the organization, the departments of the deputy secretary, chief operating officer and external affairs report to him.

While Bunch's current salary is not public yet, the Smithsonian Institution's 990 tax forms from 2020 to 2024 show that he has raked in millions of dollars, including a salary of $915,469 with $74,090 in added benefits in 2024. Other years range from $726,156 to $861,379 for his salary and up to $68,391 in added benefits.

In addition to the interview, he co-wrote a policy framework resource titled "Excellence in DEAI," an acronym for Diversity, Equity, Accessibility and Inclusion, which was written for the American Alliance of Museums. 

Bunch further elaborated on his views on diversity in this 17-page document, which says that museums should "embed responsibility and accountability for implementing DEAI policies and processes into operations, job descriptions, and performance reviews at all levels of the institution, from the board of directors, c-level executives, and senior leaders to middle managers, junior staff, and volunteers."

"DEAI is integral to excellence in museum practice. FULL STOP," Bunch wrote.

"Amid social, political and cultural polarization and clear structural racism and other forms of oppression in the United States and around the world, DEAI must be at the center of how we understand and practice excellence in our institutions," he added.

SMITHSONIAN PUSHED ‘REVOLTING’ SOCIAL ACTION TRAINING AFTER ‘WHITENESS’ CHART APOLOGY: EXPERT

Bunch’s comments, along with statements from other Smithsonian leadership members, have prompted scrutiny from the Trump administration. In a report titled Saving America’s Story, the administration raised concerns that the organization had taken on a clear political bent.

"Confirmed in the words of museum leadership, this ideological capture has moved the museum’s mission away from straightforward historical education and scholarship toward an extreme political activism that seeks to transform our country," the report reads.

For his part, Bunch has claimed that he sees himself as an apolitical actor without an agenda despite pushing for DEAI.

"What the country needs are places that are nonpartisan and safe, where people can grapple with what’s going on around them," Bunch told Smithsonian Magazine.

The Smithsonian, which was established by Congress in 1846 as an independent federal trust, depends heavily on taxpayer dollars.

TRUMP ORDERS SIGNS OUTSIDE SMITHSONIAN MUSEUM AMID ROW OVER ITS DEPICTION OF AMERICAN HISTORY

"Financially, the institution depends on the federal government for approximately two-thirds of its funding," the organization stated in its 2025 management report.

Bunch did not immediately respond to requests for comment on whether he believes his political leanings are at odds with the Smithsonian’s overall purpose or whether federal funding should prevent the organization’s employees from furthering a stated agenda.

item.title: Trump retaliates after Iran attack as expert warns regime is growing more dangerous
item.description: Trump vowed to hit Iran hard after CENTCOM confirmed all ballistic missiles targeting U.S. forces in Jordan were intercepted with no casualties reported.
item.content:encoded:
The United States resumed airstrikes inside Iran Wednesday night in retaliation for Tehran’s attempted surprise ballistic-missile attack on American forces, as an Iran expert warned that the regime has become increasingly willing to test Washington despite its weakened military capabilities.

"The strikes are a powerful response to yesterday’s attempted Iranian attack on U.S. forces based in the Middle East," U.S. Central Command said as the new operation began, according to The Associated Press.

The renewed strikes marked the first U.S. attacks inside Iran since President Donald Trump paused the bombing campaign Friday after 13 consecutive nights to allow diplomacy another chance. Iran’s missile launch shattered that brief pause and returned the conflict to direct exchanges between Washington and Tehran.

Trump had signaled the retaliation earlier Wednesday, saying the United States would hit Iran "very hard."

ARMY IDS 2 VICTIMS KILLED IN JORDAN AIR BASE ATTACK; TRUMP: IRAN WILL PAY 'MANY TIMES OVER'

Behnam Ben Taleblu, senior director of the Iran program at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, said the surprise nature of Iran’s attack reflected a significant shift in Tehran’s strategy.

"What makes this attack different is that it’s basically a surprise attack," Taleblu told Fox News Digital. "This is the Islamic Republic matching its deeds with its words," he said. "That means a more risk-tolerant, more confident, perhaps less capable, but more dangerous Iran in the Middle East."

U.S. Central Command said the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps launched multiple ballistic missiles from Iran at U.S. forces in the region at approximately 5:45 p.m. Eastern Time Tuesday. All were intercepted, and no casualties or damage were immediately reported.

Trump later vowed a forceful response, telling Fox News chief foreign correspondent Trey Yingst that the United States would be "hitting them hard" and that Iran was "going to get a beating." "We're going to beat the f---ing s--- out of them," Trump said.

US CLAWS BACK KEY CONCESSION TO IRAN AFTER FRESH ATTACKS ON COMMERCIAL SHIPS IN STRAIT OF HORMUZ

But Ben Taleblu warned that successful interceptions alone may not restore deterrence. He argued that Tehran has repeatedly learned that it can fire on American forces, absorb a U.S. response and then attempt to dictate when the exchange ends.

"The dangerous lesson for America here is that you have to treat every single Iranian missile attack, whether it was successful or not, as being successful," he said. "You can’t over-rely on technology because, ultimately, this is not a technological problem. This is a political problem."

The attack came as the nearly five-month conflict threatened to widen across the region.

Iran said it also targeted commercial tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, while the United States and Saudi Arabia jointly struck Iran-backed armed groups in Iraq following drone attacks on Saudi oil facilities. The operation marked the first time Riyadh publicly acknowledged participating in strikes alongside Washington, potentially opening a new front in the confrontation, Reuters reported. 

TWO US SERVICE MEMBERS KILLED IN IRANIAN STRIKES ON JORDAN, CENTCOM SAYS

The renewed fighting also threatens already-fragile negotiations over the Strait of Hormuz. Iran rejected an Omani proposal for joint regional management of the waterway, insisting on broader control over shipping routes through the strait.

The attack followed a far deadlier Iranian attack on U.S. forces in Jordan earlier in July. That strike hit housing used by American troops at Muwaffaq Salti Air Base, killing two U.S. service members and wounding several others.

The United States subsequently struck Iranian targets, but Ben Taleblu argued that Tehran continues to believe it can absorb retaliation, fire back and dictate when each cycle of fighting ends.

He said the United States must respond while preparing for another Iranian counterattack, warning that allowing Tehran to claim it had "closed the round" after retaliating would reinforce the regime’s belief that it can dictate the pace of the conflict.

"The U.S. certainly does need to respond, and President Trump indeed has promised to respond with some very colorful language, but it has to be prepared for the Iranian response," he said.

item.title: California mom welcomes baby in Jack in the Box parking lot after little girl couldn't wait
item.description: Michelle Cisneros says she was discharged from a local hospitall twice before delivering baby Valentina in a Jack in the Box parking lot in Orange County.
item.content:encoded:
A Southern California couple has quite the birth story to tell after their daughter made a surprise arrival in the parking lot of a Jack in the Box, where firefighters helped deliver the baby after a frantic race to the hospital.

Michelle Cisneros and Darren Campbell welcomed baby Valentina Isla Campbell last Friday after pulling into the Orange County fast-food restaurant and calling 911 when they realized they couldn't make it back to the delivery room in time.

The family says the healthy baby girl arrived 15 days before her due date, adding to their surprise.

"I thought maybe they might be Braxton Hicks," Cisneros told Fox News Digital. "But at that point my contractions were five minutes apart, and they were getting more intense, so I thought I'll just go to labor and delivery just to be safe."

DELTA FLIGHT FORCED TO DIVERT AFTER PASSENGER GOES INTO LABOR AND DELIVERS BABY MIDAIR

But amid the joy, the parents are also left wondering whether the roadside birth could have been avoided after Cisneros says she was evaluated and discharged from a nearby hospital twice before delivering baby Valentina.

Cisneros said she was monitored for about an hour at Hoag Hospital before being discharged after staff determined her cervix had not changed. She said nurses instructed her to return if her contractions became three minutes apart.

"The nurse actually told us that if my contractions were three minutes apart, to return to the hospital," Cisneros said. "We made it downstairs, and we were timing them, and they were three minutes apart."

ICE DETAINS ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT ACCUSED OF SEXUALLY ASSAULTING MINOR AFTER HOSPITAL PARKING LOT BIRTH

The couple returned to the hospital, where Michelle said she was monitored for another hour before being discharged again.

"They did end up giving me morphine because I was in a lot of pain and I could barely speak," she said. "The nurse said to continue laboring at home and then come back, that I would most likely deliver that night."

Darren Campbell said he tried to convince hospital staff not to send his wife home.

FIREFIGHTERS, POLICE PULL YOUNG WOMAN FROM SEWAGE-FILLED RAVINE AFTER DAYS TRAPPED IN 104-DEGREE HEAT

"I said, 'Look, we're not leaving. Contractions are three minutes apart,'" he recalled. "It was very dismissive of, 'You guys are okay. You guys don't have to be here. Go home and we'll see you later.'"

Campbell said he initially believed they still had enough time to make it back to the hospital before their daughter made her grand debut.

About two miles from home, they pulled into a nearby Jack in the Box parking lot and called 911 as firefighters rushed to help deliver little Valentina.

"Michelle said, 'If you can keep going, we can make it,'" he recalled. "Then the words I'll never forget — she said, 'She's coming.' That's when I told 911 I was pulling into the Jack in the Box, and that's where I knew we were in trouble."

Campbell said the arrival of firefighters brought an immediate sense of relief.

"When I heard her cry, it was just sheer relief," he said. "My worst fears were extinguished."

"The moment that I heard her cry, I instantly felt relief," Cisneros said.

Looking back, Cisneros said she hopes other expectant mothers trust their instincts.

"Women should know that they can advocate for themselves, and they know their body best," she said. "I think it's really important for medical professionals to listen to their patients more."

Campbell echoed his wife's message.

"No one knows your body better than yourself," he said. "If you've got that gut feeling, you just need to say, 'No, I know what I'm feeling.'"

The family spent several days recovering before returning home with their newest addition.

Fox News Digital reached out to Hoag Hospital for comment.

Jack in the Box also did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment after they reportedly offered the family a care package.

item.title: SEE IT: GOP senator flips script on agitators tied to pro-CCP, Singham network
item.description: Rick Scott fired back at CodePink hecklers over Gaza, Iran nuclear weapons, and Cuba sanctions in a heated Capitol Hill hallway confrontation.
item.content:encoded:
Sen. Rick Scott., R-Fla., was confronted by activists from the far-left group CodePink, accusing the senator of backing policies they claimed harmed civilians in Gaza and Cuba.

LAWMAKERS RAISE ALARM OVER NEVILLE ROY SINGHAM'S $278M NETWORK SPREADING CCP PROPAGANDA IN THE U.S.

item.title: Socialism's war on success has a new champion — and he’s running for Senate in Michigan
item.description: Abdul El-Sayed's Michigan Senate bid draws support from Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, raising alarms over socialist policies.
item.content:encoded:
The summer’s collective uplift from our nation’s 250th birthday and the United States’ role in co-hosting the World Cup has collided with the ominous spread of socialism among the American left. item.title: SEN DEB FISCHER: The left's war on the Senate and Supreme Court puts our republic at risk
item.description: The Democratic Socialists of America's platform calls to abolish the Senate and subordinate the Supreme Court to a new unicameral legislative body.
item.content:encoded:
The Democratic Socialists of America recently rolled out a policy platform wrapped in delusional promises — free government-run healthcare, the abolition of the police and prison systems and the defunding of our military. While those proposals sound crazy enough, something far more radical is buried underneath: a call to abolish the Senate and subordinate the presidency and the Supreme Court to a new unicameral body that would choose and control the executive and judicial branches.

That proposal is not just unserious — it is a direct assault on the Constitution. The attacks on the Supreme Court's legitimacy and the calls to abolish the Senate spring from the same impulse: impatience with constitutional limits on political power. When institutions become obstacles to ideological goals, the answer should never be to tear them down.

That dangerous mindset has consequences beyond political rhetoric. Our Supreme Court justices and their families have been subject to escalating threats in recent years. 

DSA CO-CHAIR EMBRACES ABOLISHING SENATE, ICE, BORDERS AS DEMOCRATIC INFIGHTING ESCALATES

During a recent Senate Appropriations Committee hearing, I heard directly from Justices Amy Coney Barrett and Elena Kagan. Both described a security posture that has not kept pace with the threats they now face. In fact, after the leak of the court’s decision to overturn Roe v. Wade, Justice Barrett came home from work wearing a bulletproof vest given to her by her security detail. She recounted placing the vest on a table and having to explain to her 12-year-old son what it was and why she had it.

No justice should fear for their safety because they faithfully discharge their constitutional duty. Yet instead of treating this as the urgent, nonpartisan security matter it is, we continue to hear rhetoric that attacks the very legitimacy of the court as an institution. In 2020, Sen. Chuck Schumer said Justices Brett Kavanaugh and Neil Gorsuch would "pay the price" if they acted to restrict abortion. His comments were inappropriate and dangerous. Unfortunately, this sentiment has continued to proliferate and fuel physical threats. More recently, congressional Democrats have called the Supreme Court "corrupt," "rigged" and "a disgrace."

Criticism of the court's decisions is part of a healthy democracy. Justice Kagan said as much herself. But there is a clear difference between criticizing a ruling and undermining the legitimacy of the institution or inciting threats against those who serve on it.

JUSTICE NEIL GORSUCH BREAKS SILENCE ON VIOLENT THREATS AGAINST JUDICIARY, SUPREME COURT LEAKS

The same impatience animates the DSA's call to abolish the Senate. The Senate provides a necessary counterbalance to the House of Representatives. It balances power by granting each state equal representation, protecting smaller states from being steamrolled by larger ones. Because senators serve staggered six-year terms, the body is insulated from drastic swings in public opinion. That deliberate friction is what has allowed the republic to endure for generations.

The three branches of government conceived by the Founders have served our democracy well. Republicans and Democrats alike should reject calls to dismantle our constitutional order.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Now is the time to reaffirm our commitment to those institutions. Congress can ensure that Supreme Court justices have the security resources necessary to carry out their duties without fear or intimidation. 

I will continue making this a priority through my role on the Appropriations Committee. But we need every American to reject the DSA’s reckless calls to dismantle the constitutional framework that has preserved our republic for 250 years.

The answer to political disagreement is not to weaken the Constitution — it is to defend it.
